claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the compared quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has more extensive or stronger local chemical short-range order than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Short-range order in the quinary alloy creates nanoscale obstacles to dislocation motion.
Dislocation-obstructing short-range-order features are less pronounced in the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The additional constituent in the quinary alloy promotes stronger local chemical short-range order.
Reduced chemical complexity in the quaternary and ternary subsets causes a lower degree of short-range order.
A lower degree of short-range order produces less obstruction to dislocation motion.
Greater short-range-order-mediated obstruction to dislocation motion gives the quinary alloy a higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have reduced strain hardening.
The predicted reductions in yield strength and strain hardening arise from diminished short-range order in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
All compared alloys remain single-phase FCC throughout mechanical testing.
Atom probe tomography can quantify the local chemical short-range order relevant to the proposed mechanism.
In situ transmission electron microscopy can reveal whether dislocations interact with the proposed short-range-order features.
